screens.title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we explore IAM, the security foundation that determines who or what can access AWS resources and which actions they may take. IAM is not limited to human users; services and applications assume identities too. You will learn the core building blocks — IAM users, groups, roles, and policies — and see how they interact to grant temporary or long-lived permissions. We’ll emphasize why roles are preferred for AWS services, how policies express permissions in JSON, and why the principle of least privilege must guide every decision. We’ll also cover Multi-Factor Authentication and common configuration mistakes that create unnecessary risk. A concrete hands-on walkthrough will show how to create a role for an EC2 instance to read only a single S3 bucket, eliminating embedded credentials. By the end of the module you should be able to choose between identity-based and resource-based policies, design a minimal-permission policy, and apply MFA and group-based administration to reduce operational friction. Think of IAM as both the gatekeeper and the auditor: configure it carefully so your systems can operate securely and your audits are simple. What is one permission you can remove today to shrink your attack surface?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: IAM defines identities (users, groups, roles) and rules (policies) that control access — design with least privilege and prefer roles for AWS services.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Fundamentals
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

IAM Fundamentals

Understand identities, policies, and secure practices that reduce exposure and enable safe automation.

In this lesson
Users, Groups, Roles, Policies
Foundational building blocks and how they fit together.
Coming up
Least privilege & MFA
Practical rules to harden access and reduce blast radius.
Hands-on
Role for EC2 with S3 read-only
A safe pattern that avoids long-lived credentials on instances.
Concept Map
Identities
User: named identity with credentials
Group: collection of users
Role: assumable identity for temporary permissions
Policies & Practices
Policies express allowed or denied actions on resources. Best practices include MFA, least privilege, roles for services, and groups for admin ease.
Quick Reference
Root user
Avoid daily use; enable MFA and protect credentials.
Roles for services
Preferred over embedded keys for EC2, Lambda, and ECS.
Explore Key Topics
Policy Types
Identity-based, resource-based, AWS vs customer managed, and inline policies.
Least Privilege
Grant only required actions on specific resources; avoid wildcards.
MFA & Root Safety
Enable MFA for root and privileged accounts; avoid root keys in operations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this session we target four practical competencies tied to IAM. First, you will be able to explain the core IAM components — users, groups, roles, and policies — and describe how they combine to protect resources. That means knowing what an IAM user represents, why groups simplify management, and how roles deliver temporary permissions to services. Second, you will differentiate policy types: identity-based versus resource-based, AWS managed versus customer managed, and inline policies. Knowing these differences helps you choose where to attach permissions and how to structure accounts securely. Third, you will apply the principle of least privilege when assigning permissions. This includes crafting narrow actions and resource ARNs instead of using wildcards. Practically, you’ll learn to limit permissions to specific S3 buckets, actions, and conditions. Fourth, you will configure MFA for both root and IAM users and identify common mistakes and remediation steps. Enforcing MFA reduces risk from compromised credentials and is a simple, high-impact control. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can check your settings and confirm secure outcomes. As you work, ask: which permission can I revoke right now to make the environment safer?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: This continuation expands the objectives with practical verification steps and mental models you will apply. First, practice creating and rotating access keys for programmatic users and know when to avoid them entirely; rotating keys and monitoring usage prevents credential sprawl. Second, manage permissions at scale with groups and customer-managed policies so policies are reusable and auditable. Reuse reduces configuration drift and simplifies incident response. Third, design roles with trust policies for EC2, Lambda, or federated users so services obtain temporary credentials instead of storing long-lived keys. A sample trust relationship for EC2 lets the EC2 service assume a role via the security token service. Fourth, learn to review policies and identify overly broad statements such as actions or resources with a wildcard. Use tooling and periodic review to detect unintended access. Each objective includes a quick verification: list attached policies, inspect trust relationships, and test an assumed role from an instance. These checks help you confirm that intentions match reality. As you progress, consider this question: can you describe the minimum permission set needed for a single service without granting extra actions?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Learning Objectives
Practical verification cards
Verify Keys
Rotate access keys regularly and prefer roles for services. Confirm only required programs have keys and record last rotated dates.
Group Management
Attach policies to groups, not individual users, to ensure consistent permissions across teams and easier offboarding.
Trust Policies
Design trust policy documents that explicitly allow the correct AWS service to assume the role; keep trust narrow to the service and account.
Policy Reviews
Scan for wildcards in actions and resources. If s3:* or arn:aws:s3:::* appears, evaluate whether it can be narrowed to exact actions and ARNs.
Check your understanding
Try these quick mental checks:
  • Can the service run without long-lived credentials?
  • Does any policy include an unnecessary wildcard?
  • Is MFA enforced for privileged accounts?

screens.title: What is an IAM User?
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM user is a distinct identity in your AWS account that represents a person or a service. A user has credentials: a password for console access and optional programmatic access keys for command-line or A P I calls. Use users for human operators who require persistent accounts, but avoid embedding access keys into systems where possible. A practical example: create an IAM user for a developer who needs console access and attach them to a group that grants the appropriate permissions. Always enable Multi-Factor Authentication for users with elevated privileges. When you issue access keys, plan to rotate them and monitor their use. A frequent misconception is thinking that every program or script needs its own user with long-lived keys. Instead, prefer roles for services and only issue keys to applications that cannot assume a role. For programmatic processes that must run outside AWS, create a narrowly scoped user and rotate keys often. Key takeaway: use IAM users for people and external systems that truly need persistent credentials, secure them with strong passwords and MFA, rotate keys, and keep access minimal. What user credential would you rotate this week to reduce risk?

keyIdea.text: IAM User = persistent identity with credentials; use for humans or external systems that need long-lived access, secured by MFA and key rotation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is an IAM User?
Definition

IAM User explained

An IAM user is a named account for a person or external service. It can hold a console password and access keys for programmatic access. Best practice: prefer MFA and rotate keys.

Concrete example
A developer account with console access and membership in a group that grants EC2 management rights. The user has MFA enabled and keys rotated monthly.
Common misconception
Treating users as the default for automated services. Instead, use roles for AWS services to avoid long-lived credentials on instances.
Key Takeaway

Use IAM users for people or external systems; enforce MFA, rotate keys, and minimize privileges.

Credential Examples
Console password: human access Programmatic keys: access key ID + secret access key Rotate keys: replace old keys and remove unused ones
Quick checklist
  • Enable MFA for user accounts.
  • Attach permissions via groups, not directly.
  • Avoid embedding keys on EC2; use roles instead.
Mnemonic
User = Person. Remember: users represent named human or external identities.

screens.title: IAM Groups: Manage users at scale
screens.narratorSegment: IAM groups let you attach policies once and give the resulting permissions to every user in the group. This pattern drastically reduces administrative effort for onboarding and offboarding. For example, an EC2Admins group can hold permissions to start, stop, and manage instances; adding a new administrator is a matter of placing their user in that group. A common pitfall is attaching policies directly to users rather than to groups; this creates drift and makes audits difficult. Another issue arises when groups are overly broad: don't create a single 'AllEmployees' group with many permissions. Instead, create focused groups like 'S3Developers' and 'BillingReaders' to limit access. When you need custom combinations, prefer customer-managed policies attached to groups rather than duplicating inline policies across users. Using groups also helps you implement separation of duties: combine small groups to form the exact permissions a person needs. The practical outcome: consistent permissions, simpler reviews, and fewer mistakes. Reflect: which groups in your account would benefit from a narrower policy? IAM Groups: Manage users at scale means use groups to assign reusable policies to multiple users; avoid direct user attachments and overly broad groups.. In practical terms, groups simplify permission management across teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Groups
Why groups?

Group-based permission management

Attach policies to a group once and every member inherits those permissions. This reduces repetitive tasks and human errors.

Scenario
Add a new EC2 operator: place their user in the EC2Admins group to grant consistent instance management permissions.
Pitfall
Attaching many policies directly to users leads to drift. Use groups to keep policy assignments centralized and auditable.
Best practice
Use customer-managed policies attached to groups for reuse and clearer ownership.
Group design patterns
Build small, focused groups that map to real responsibilities. Combine groups for users who span roles rather than creating many one-off policies.
Example cards
EC2Admins
Manage EC2 instances in specified accounts or regions.
S3Developers
Read and list objects in a defined bucket, not all buckets.
Key Takeaway

Groups reduce complexity: attach policies to groups for consistent permissions and easier audits.

screens.title: IAM Roles: Temporary credentials for services
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM role is an identity you can assume to obtain temporary credentials. Roles are the recommended way to grant permissions to AWS services and federated users because they remove the need to store long-lived access keys on instances or containers. For example, an EC2 instance that needs to read an S3 bucket should assume an EC2 role with s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket permissions on the specific bucket. When the instance assumes that role, the AWS security token service issues temporary credentials with an expiration, limiting exposure if the instance is compromised. Roles also support trust policies that define which principals may assume them — commonly the ec2. amazonaws. com service principal for instances and external identity providers for federated users. A common misunderstanding is treating roles as static accounts; instead, they are assumed at runtime and grant transient access. Key practice: craft narrow policies for the role’s permissions and restrict the trust policy to the intended principal. This reduces blast radius and aligns with least privilege. Consider: can your services work with temporary permissions rather than embedded keys? IAM Roles: Temporary credentials for services means roles provide temporary credentials via assumption; use them for services and federated users to avoid long-lived keys.. In practical terms, how roles eliminate long-lived keys and enable secure service access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Roles
Definition

Role = assumable identity

Roles are assumed at runtime and provide temporary credentials. They include permissions and a trust policy that governs who may assume the role.

Example trust policy (concept)
A trust policy grants ec2.amazonaws.com permission to assume the role for EC2 instances.
Concrete example
An EC2 instance assumes EC2S3ReaderRole to list and read objects from a single S3 bucket. No access keys are stored on the instance.
Key Takeaway

Prefer roles for AWS services; design narrow permissions and restrict trust relationships.

Misconceptions
  • Roles are permanent accounts. (No: they are assumed and grant temporary credentials.)
  • Any service can assume any role. (No: trust policies limit which principals may assume a role.)
Design checklist
  • Limit actions to required API calls.
  • Scope resources to the minimal ARNs needed.
  • Restrict trust to the exact service principal or external provider.

screens.title: IAM Policies: Structure and intent
screens.narratorSegment: IAM policies are the language of permissions in AWS. A policy is a JSON document that contains statements declaring whether actions are allowed or denied for specified resources and conditions. The key fields are Effect, Action, Resource, and optional Condition. For example, a policy can Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/* while Denying s3:DeleteObject. Policy types vary: identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles; resource-based policies attach directly to resources like an S3 bucket; AWS managed policies are predefined by AWS; customer-managed policies are authored by you; inline policies are embedded into a single identity. A frequent confusion is assuming managed policies are always safe. In practice, AWS managed policies may grant broader permissions than your use case requires. Therefore, create customer-managed policies scoped to exact actions and resources. Another common pitfall is using wildcards in Action or Resource without understanding the blast radius. Key takeaway: write clear, minimal policy statements and use conditions to tighten access further. How would you narrow a broad s3:* statement in your account? IAM Policies: Structure and intent means policies use effect, action, resource, and condition to state permissions; prefer narrow, customer-managed policies over broad managed ones.. In practical terms, policies are json documents that allow or deny actions on resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Policies use Effect, Action, Resource, and Condition to state permissions; prefer narrow, customer-managed policies over broad managed ones.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Policies
Structure
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject","s3:ListBucket"],
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket","arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"]
  }]
}
This example allows listing and reading objects from a single S3 bucket. Note the separate bucket ARN and object ARN.
Key Takeaway

Use Effect, Action, Resource, and Condition deliberately; scope ARNs and actions to minimize risk.

Policy types
Identity-based
Attach to users, groups, or roles to define what that identity can do.
Resource-based
Attach directly to resources like S3 buckets to control which principals can access the resource.
Managed vs Inline
AWS managed policies are convenient but may be broad; customer-managed policies give fine-grained control; inline policies tie a policy lifecycle to an identity.

screens.title: Identity-based vs Resource-based Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between identity-based and resource-based policies affects control and delegation. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles and state what that identity can do across resources. Resource-based policies attach directly to the resource, allowing you to declare which principals may access that specific resource — a typical example is an S3 bucket policy granting a different AWS account read access. Use identity-based policies when you manage permissions from the identity side; use resource-based policies when resource owners must explicitly grant access to external principals or accounts. AWS managed policies are helpful for rapid setup but may be broader than necessary; customer-managed policies provide precise, reusable control. Inline policies are convenient for one-off bindings but do not scale well. A common misconception is that resource-based policies replace identity-based ones; they complement each other. When both exist, policy evaluation combines them and denies win over allows. Key takeaway: attach policies at the point that best matches ownership and operational needs while keeping the effective permission set minimal. Ask: who owns the resource and which model reduces administration burden while keeping security tight?

keyIdea.text: Identity-based policies define what an identity can do; resource-based policies define who can access a resource. Use the model aligned with ownership and delegation needs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Policy Comparison
Identity-based

Attach to users, groups, roles

Controls what an identity can do. Best for centrally managing permissions for teams and services within your account.
Use when
Permissions follow the person or service, and you want reuse across multiple resources.
Example
S3ReadOnly policy attached to a role assumed by multiple EC2 instances.
Resource-based

Attach to the resource itself

Best when resource owners need to grant access to external principals or accounts directly on the resource.
Use when
You need to grant cross-account access or limit who may access a specific bucket or queue.
Example
An S3 bucket policy granting read access to an external account's principal.
Key Takeaway

Use identity-based policies for people and services you control; use resource-based policies to delegate access to external principals or cross-account scenarios.

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task, and no more. To apply it practically, follow a short process: first, define the minimal actions required by the user or service — list exact A P I calls or console operations needed. Second, scope resources to precise ARNs rather than wildcards. For example, prefer arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/* over arn:aws:s3:::*. Third, include conditions to restrict usage, such as IP address ranges, MFA requirement, or time windows when relevant. Fourth, assign those permissions to a role or group, test access by attempting the permitted operations and attempting forbidden ones, and iterate to remove any remaining excess. Fifth, review and rotate credentials and policies regularly. A common mistake is granting AdministratorAccess or broad s3:* because it's faster; this expands your attack surface and makes incident response harder. Using tools such as IAM Access Analyzer can help find unintended access, but your initial design is what limits risk. Key takeaway: a small, iterative process yields low-risk permissions that are easy to audit and maintain. Which permission group in your account could you narrow today?

keyIdea.title: Least privilege steps
keyIdea.text: Define required actions, scope ARNs, add conditions, assign to roles/groups, test, and review regularly to maintain minimal permissions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Least Privilege
Five-step process
1
Identify required actions
List exact API calls or console operations the identity needs, for example s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket.
2
Scope resources
Use specific ARNs, target a single bucket or resource path, and avoid global wildcards.
3
Add conditions
Restrict by IP, require MFA, or limit by time where appropriate to tighten access.
4
Assign and test
Attach the policy to a role or group, test allowed and denied actions, and iterate until minimal access is achieved.
5
Review regularly
Use logs and tools to review permissions and rotate credentials to avoid drift and stale access.
Analogy
Think of permissions like keys to rooms. Grant access only to the rooms needed to do a job, not to the entire building.
Common mistake
Using broad policies such as AdministratorAccess for convenience. This creates large blast radiuses and complicates audits.

screens.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-Factor Authentication requires two forms of verification and dramatically reduces the risk from compromised passwords. For AWS accounts, enabling MFA on the root user is non-negotiable; the root user has full account privileges and should rarely be used. For IAM users with elevated privileges, require MFA so that possession of a password alone is not enough to access sensitive functions. Common MFA options include virtual authenticators such as smartphone apps that generate time-based codes or hardware MFA devices. In practice: enable MFA on the root account, require MFA for administrators, and include an MFA condition in sensitive policies to enforce it programmatically. A common misconception is believing MFA prevents all compromise; it greatly reduces risk but must be combined with least privilege and key rotation. Also plan for secure MFA device recovery procedures so users can regain access without exposing other credentials. Key takeaway: MFA is a simple, high-impact control — enable it for root and privileged users and enforce it where critical actions occur. Who on your team should have MFA configured today? Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) means mfa adds a second verification factor; enable it for root and privileged users and enforce it for critical actions via policy conditions.. In practical terms, add a second form of verification for root and iam users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › MFA
Why MFA matters
It prevents single-credential compromise from resulting in account takeover, especially for highly privileged accounts.
Enable MFA on the root account immediately. Enforce MFA for administrative roles and sensitive API calls. Consider using MFA as a condition in policies so certain actions require a second factor even for authenticated users.
Example
Require MFA to delete production resources by adding an MFA condition to the policy that denies actions unless MFA is present.
Recovery planning
Have documented device recovery processes to avoid lockout while keeping security controls intact.
Quick actions
  • Enable root MFA now.
  • Require MFA for admin users and roles.
  • Add MFA condition to sensitive policies where possible.
Key Takeaway

MFA significantly reduces the attack surface for privileged accounts; enable it and include it in policy conditions for critical operations.

screens.title: Common IAM Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Many IAM misconfigurations come from shortcuts: attaching broad policies like AdministratorAccess, using wildcards for resources or actions, storing access keys on instances, and not enforcing MFA. These increase your attack surface and complicate audits. Best practices counter these errors: never use the root account in daily operations; enable MFA for root and privileged users; use roles for AWS services instead of embedded keys; attach policies to groups and use customer-managed policies for reuse; and review permissions regularly. A concrete mistake to avoid is giving an EC2 instance AdministratorAccess for convenience. Instead, create a role with only necessary S3 and CloudWatch permissions and attach it to the instance. Regularly review CloudTrail logs for unusual IAM activity and run policy analysis tools to find overly permissive statements. Automate periodic reviews and implement a rotation schedule for keys. The final takeaway: design small, auditable permissions and treat IAM as a living configuration that requires regular maintenance. Ask yourself: which of these practices can you automate this week to reduce risk? Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Mistakes & Best Practices
Common mistakes
  • Using root for daily tasks or storing root access keys.
  • Attaching AdministratorAccess where narrow policies suffice.
  • Embedding long-lived keys on instances instead of using roles.
  • Not enforcing MFA for privileged users.
Best practices
  • Create an administrative IAM user and secure the root account with MFA.
  • Use roles for services, groups for users, and customer-managed policies for reuse.
  • Rotate keys and monitor CloudTrail for unusual behavior.
Pro tip
Automate policy reviews and use IAM Access Analyzer to detect unintended access. Treat IAM as config that must be maintained, not set-and-forget.
Common mistake alert
Avoid attaching wide policies like s3:* or AdministratorAccess for convenience; they expand attack surface and complicate investigations.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create an IAM Role for EC2 with S3 Read-Only Access
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the exact steps to create an S3 bucket, a narrow read-only policy, an EC2 role with an appropriate trust policy, attach the policy, and launch an instance that assumes the role. First, create the S3 bucket and upload a test object so you have a resource to grant access to. Second, author a policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the specific bucket ARNs. Third, create a trust policy that allows the EC2 service principal to assume the role. Fourth, create the role and attach the custom policy to it. Fifth, launch an EC2 instance and select the new role during configuration. Finally, SSH into the instance and test that you can list and copy objects from the bucket while attempts to list all S3 buckets should fail. A common misconception is that attaching a policy to the role automatically grants account-wide access; ensure the policy resource ARNs are explicit. Use these steps as a template and replace the bucket name with your unique identifier. After testing, remove unused keys and review the role’s permissions to keep privileges minimal. How would you change the policy if the application also needed to write logs to CloudWatch?

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Create a specific bucket, a custom policy scoped to that bucket, an EC2 trust role, and verify the instance can read the bucket but cannot list all buckets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Hands-on: EC2 Role for S3
Terminal steps (conceptual)
Follow these steps and substitute your unique bucket name where needed. The commands below are the exact sequence used in the activity description.
# 1. Create S3 bucket and upload a test file
aws s3 mb s3://my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123 --region us-east-1
echo "Hello from S3!" > index.html
aws s3 cp index.html s3://my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123/

# 2. Policy json (s3-readonly-policy.json)
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123", "arn:aws:s3:::my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123/*" ] } ] }

# 3. Create policy via CLI
aws iam create-policy --policy-name S3AppReadOnlyPolicy --policy-document file://s3-readonly-policy.json

# 4. Trust policy for EC2 (ec2-trust-policy.json)
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] }

# 5. Create role and attach policy
aws iam create-role --role-name EC2S3ReaderRole --assume-role-policy-document file://ec2-trust-policy.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name EC2S3ReaderRole --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:policy/S3AppReadOnlyPolicy

# 6. Launch EC2 and select EC2S3ReaderRole

# 7. On the instance, test access
aws s3 ls s3://my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123/
aws s3 cp s3://my-sysops-app-data-unique-name-123/index.html .
# This should fail:
aws s3 ls
Remember to replace YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID and use a globally unique bucket name. After testing, remove any temporary resources and confirm the role’s policy grants only the required actions.
Example explanation
The created role allows EC2 instances to obtain temporary credentials and read objects from only the specified bucket. Attempts to list all buckets should fail because the policy does not grant s3:ListAllMyBuckets.
Key Takeaway

Use a role with a narrowly scoped policy to avoid long-lived keys on instances; test that only the intended bucket is accessible.

screens.title: Designing an IAM Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing an IAM strategy starts with mapping actors to identities and determining where permissions should live. Identify human users, automated services, and external federated users. For humans, create IAM users or rely on federation and manage their permissions via groups. For AWS services, prefer roles with trust policies and short-lived credentials. Use customer-managed policies for predictable reuse and attach them to groups or roles; reserve inline policies for rare, tightly-scoped use cases where the policy lifecycle should be bound to that identity. Define a policy lifecycle that includes authoring, review, testing, and scheduled rotation. Automate discovery and review using logs and IAM tooling to identify stale or broad permissions. Plan for emergencies by creating a restricted break-glass role with AdministratorAccess that is strictly audited and protected by MFA. Finally, include training and documented procedures for onboarding and offboarding so permissions match staff responsibilities at all times. A common misconception is that IAM is a one-time setup; in reality it requires continuous governance. Key takeaway: an IAM strategy maps identities to minimal permissions, centralizes reusable policies, and enforces reviews and MFA to maintain security over time.

keyIdea.text: Map actors, prefer roles for services, centralize policies in groups, automate reviews, and maintain a break-glass plan with strict protections.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Strategy
Strategy checklist
Map actors to identities
Categorize humans, services, and federated users and choose users, roles, or federation accordingly.
Centralize policies
Keep reusable policies as customer-managed and attach them to groups or roles for clarity and reuse.
Automate reviews
Schedule policy reviews, scan for wildcards, and use logs to identify unused or excessive permissions.
Include a documented break-glass process: a limited-scope administrative role protected by MFA and monitored for use. Train teams on onboarding and offboarding so permissions match responsibilities from day one.
Operational flow
  1. Define required actions per role.
  2. Create customer-managed policies.
  3. Attach to groups or roles; test access.
  4. Schedule reviews and rotate keys.
Key Takeaway

An IAM strategy combines mapping, centralized policies, automation, and governance to maintain secure and auditable permissions.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we explore IAM, the security foundation that determines who or what can access AWS resources and which actions they may take. IAM is not limited to human users; services and applications assume identities too. You will learn the core building blocks — IAM users, groups, roles, and policies — and see how they interact to grant temporary or long-lived permissions. We’ll emphasize why roles are preferred for AWS services, how policies express permissions in JSON, and why the principle of least privilege must guide every decision. We’ll also cover Multi-Factor Authentication and common configuration mistakes that create unnecessary risk. A concrete hands-on walkthrough will show how to create a role for an EC2 instance to read only a single S3 bucket, eliminating embedded credentials. By the end of the module you should be able to choose between identity-based and resource-based policies, design a minimal-permission policy, and apply MFA and group-based administration to reduce operational friction. Think of IAM as both the gatekeeper and the auditor: configure it carefully so your systems can operate securely and your audits are simple. What is one permission you can remove today to shrink your attack surface?

In this session we target four practical competencies tied to IAM. First, you will be able to explain the core IAM components — users, groups, roles, and policies — and describe how they combine to protect resources. That means knowing what an IAM user represents, why groups simplify management, and how roles deliver temporary permissions to services. Second, you will differentiate policy types: identity-based versus resource-based, AWS managed versus customer managed, and inline policies. Knowing these differences helps you choose where to attach permissions and how to structure accounts securely. Third, you will apply the principle of least privilege when assigning permissions. This includes crafting narrow actions and resource ARNs instead of using wildcards. Practically, you’ll learn to limit permissions to specific S3 buckets, actions, and conditions. Fourth, you will configure MFA for both root and IAM users and identify common mistakes and remediation steps. Enforcing MFA reduces risk from compromised credentials and is a simple, high-impact control. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can check your settings and confirm secure outcomes. As you work, ask: which permission can I revoke right now to make the environment safer?

This continuation expands the objectives with practical verification steps and mental models you will apply. First, practice creating and rotating access keys for programmatic users and know when to avoid them entirely; rotating keys and monitoring usage prevents credential sprawl. Second, manage permissions at scale with groups and customer-managed policies so policies are reusable and auditable. Reuse reduces configuration drift and simplifies incident response. Third, design roles with trust policies for EC2, Lambda, or federated users so services obtain temporary credentials instead of storing long-lived keys. A sample trust relationship for EC2 lets the EC2 service assume a role via the security token service. Fourth, learn to review policies and identify overly broad statements such as actions or resources with a wildcard. Use tooling and periodic review to detect unintended access. Each objective includes a quick verification: list attached policies, inspect trust relationships, and test an assumed role from an instance. These checks help you confirm that intentions match reality. As you progress, consider this question: can you describe the minimum permission set needed for a single service without granting extra actions?

An IAM user is a distinct identity in your AWS account that represents a person or a service. A user has credentials: a password for console access and optional programmatic access keys for command-line or A P I calls. Use users for human operators who require persistent accounts, but avoid embedding access keys into systems where possible. A practical example: create an IAM user for a developer who needs console access and attach them to a group that grants the appropriate permissions. Always enable Multi-Factor Authentication for users with elevated privileges. When you issue access keys, plan to rotate them and monitor their use. A frequent misconception is thinking that every program or script needs its own user with long-lived keys. Instead, prefer roles for services and only issue keys to applications that cannot assume a role. For programmatic processes that must run outside AWS, create a narrowly scoped user and rotate keys often. Key takeaway: use IAM users for people and external systems that truly need persistent credentials, secure them with strong passwords and MFA, rotate keys, and keep access minimal. What user credential would you rotate this week to reduce risk?

IAM groups let you attach policies once and give the resulting permissions to every user in the group. This pattern drastically reduces administrative effort for onboarding and offboarding. For example, an EC2Admins group can hold permissions to start, stop, and manage instances; adding a new administrator is a matter of placing their user in that group. A common pitfall is attaching policies directly to users rather than to groups; this creates drift and makes audits difficult. Another issue arises when groups are overly broad: don't create a single 'AllEmployees' group with many permissions. Instead, create focused groups like 'S3Developers' and 'BillingReaders' to limit access. When you need custom combinations, prefer customer-managed policies attached to groups rather than duplicating inline policies across users. Using groups also helps you implement separation of duties: combine small groups to form the exact permissions a person needs. The practical outcome: consistent permissions, simpler reviews, and fewer mistakes. Reflect: which groups in your account would benefit from a narrower policy? IAM Groups: Manage users at scale means use groups to assign reusable policies to multiple users; avoid direct user attachments and overly broad groups.. In practical terms, groups simplify permission management across teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An IAM role is an identity you can assume to obtain temporary credentials. Roles are the recommended way to grant permissions to AWS services and federated users because they remove the need to store long-lived access keys on instances or containers. For example, an EC2 instance that needs to read an S3 bucket should assume an EC2 role with s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket permissions on the specific bucket. When the instance assumes that role, the AWS security token service issues temporary credentials with an expiration, limiting exposure if the instance is compromised. Roles also support trust policies that define which principals may assume them — commonly the ec2. amazonaws. com service principal for instances and external identity providers for federated users. A common misunderstanding is treating roles as static accounts; instead, they are assumed at runtime and grant transient access. Key practice: craft narrow policies for the role’s permissions and restrict the trust policy to the intended principal. This reduces blast radius and aligns with least privilege. Consider: can your services work with temporary permissions rather than embedded keys? IAM Roles: Temporary credentials for services means roles provide temporary credentials via assumption; use them for services and federated users to avoid long-lived keys.. In practical terms, how roles eliminate long-lived keys and enable secure service access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IAM policies are the language of permissions in AWS. A policy is a JSON document that contains statements declaring whether actions are allowed or denied for specified resources and conditions. The key fields are Effect, Action, Resource, and optional Condition. For example, a policy can Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/* while Denying s3:DeleteObject. Policy types vary: identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles; resource-based policies attach directly to resources like an S3 bucket; AWS managed policies are predefined by AWS; customer-managed policies are authored by you; inline policies are embedded into a single identity. A frequent confusion is assuming managed policies are always safe. In practice, AWS managed policies may grant broader permissions than your use case requires. Therefore, create customer-managed policies scoped to exact actions and resources. Another common pitfall is using wildcards in Action or Resource without understanding the blast radius. Key takeaway: write clear, minimal policy statements and use conditions to tighten access further. How would you narrow a broad s3:* statement in your account? IAM Policies: Structure and intent means policies use effect, action, resource, and condition to state permissions; prefer narrow, customer-managed policies over broad managed ones.. In practical terms, policies are json documents that allow or deny actions on resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between identity-based and resource-based policies affects control and delegation. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles and state what that identity can do across resources. Resource-based policies attach directly to the resource, allowing you to declare which principals may access that specific resource — a typical example is an S3 bucket policy granting a different AWS account read access. Use identity-based policies when you manage permissions from the identity side; use resource-based policies when resource owners must explicitly grant access to external principals or accounts. AWS managed policies are helpful for rapid setup but may be broader than necessary; customer-managed policies provide precise, reusable control. Inline policies are convenient for one-off bindings but do not scale well. A common misconception is that resource-based policies replace identity-based ones; they complement each other. When both exist, policy evaluation combines them and denies win over allows. Key takeaway: attach policies at the point that best matches ownership and operational needs while keeping the effective permission set minimal. Ask: who owns the resource and which model reduces administration burden while keeping security tight?

The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task, and no more. To apply it practically, follow a short process: first, define the minimal actions required by the user or service — list exact A P I calls or console operations needed. Second, scope resources to precise ARNs rather than wildcards. For example, prefer arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/* over arn:aws:s3:::*. Third, include conditions to restrict usage, such as IP address ranges, MFA requirement, or time windows when relevant. Fourth, assign those permissions to a role or group, test access by attempting the permitted operations and attempting forbidden ones, and iterate to remove any remaining excess. Fifth, review and rotate credentials and policies regularly. A common mistake is granting AdministratorAccess or broad s3:* because it's faster; this expands your attack surface and makes incident response harder. Using tools such as IAM Access Analyzer can help find unintended access, but your initial design is what limits risk. Key takeaway: a small, iterative process yields low-risk permissions that are easy to audit and maintain. Which permission group in your account could you narrow today?

Multi-Factor Authentication requires two forms of verification and dramatically reduces the risk from compromised passwords. For AWS accounts, enabling MFA on the root user is non-negotiable; the root user has full account privileges and should rarely be used. For IAM users with elevated privileges, require MFA so that possession of a password alone is not enough to access sensitive functions. Common MFA options include virtual authenticators such as smartphone apps that generate time-based codes or hardware MFA devices. In practice: enable MFA on the root account, require MFA for administrators, and include an MFA condition in sensitive policies to enforce it programmatically. A common misconception is believing MFA prevents all compromise; it greatly reduces risk but must be combined with least privilege and key rotation. Also plan for secure MFA device recovery procedures so users can regain access without exposing other credentials. Key takeaway: MFA is a simple, high-impact control — enable it for root and privileged users and enforce it where critical actions occur. Who on your team should have MFA configured today? Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) means mfa adds a second verification factor; enable it for root and privileged users and enforce it for critical actions via policy conditions.. In practical terms, add a second form of verification for root and iam users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Many IAM misconfigurations come from shortcuts: attaching broad policies like AdministratorAccess, using wildcards for resources or actions, storing access keys on instances, and not enforcing MFA. These increase your attack surface and complicate audits. Best practices counter these errors: never use the root account in daily operations; enable MFA for root and privileged users; use roles for AWS services instead of embedded keys; attach policies to groups and use customer-managed policies for reuse; and review permissions regularly. A concrete mistake to avoid is giving an EC2 instance AdministratorAccess for convenience. Instead, create a role with only necessary S3 and CloudWatch permissions and attach it to the instance. Regularly review CloudTrail logs for unusual IAM activity and run policy analysis tools to find overly permissive statements. Automate periodic reviews and implement a rotation schedule for keys. The final takeaway: design small, auditable permissions and treat IAM as a living configuration that requires regular maintenance. Ask yourself: which of these practices can you automate this week to reduce risk? This hands-on walkthrough follows the exact steps to create an S3 bucket, a narrow read-only policy, an EC2 role with an appropriate trust policy, attach the policy, and launch an instance that assumes the role. First, create the S3 bucket and upload a test object so you have a resource to grant access to. Second, author a policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the specific bucket ARNs. Third, create a trust policy that allows the EC2 service principal to assume the role. Fourth, create the role and attach the custom policy to it. Fifth, launch an EC2 instance and select the new role during configuration. Finally, SSH into the instance and test that you can list and copy objects from the bucket while attempts to list all S3 buckets should fail. A common misconception is that attaching a policy to the role automatically grants account-wide access; ensure the policy resource ARNs are explicit. Use these steps as a template and replace the bucket name with your unique identifier. After testing, remove unused keys and review the role’s permissions to keep privileges minimal. How would you change the policy if the application also needed to write logs to CloudWatch?

Designing an IAM strategy starts with mapping actors to identities and determining where permissions should live. Identify human users, automated services, and external federated users. For humans, create IAM users or rely on federation and manage their permissions via groups. For AWS services, prefer roles with trust policies and short-lived credentials. Use customer-managed policies for predictable reuse and attach them to groups or roles; reserve inline policies for rare, tightly-scoped use cases where the policy lifecycle should be bound to that identity. Define a policy lifecycle that includes authoring, review, testing, and scheduled rotation. Automate discovery and review using logs and IAM tooling to identify stale or broad permissions. Plan for emergencies by creating a restricted break-glass role with AdministratorAccess that is strictly audited and protected by MFA. Finally, include training and documented procedures for onboarding and offboarding so permissions match staff responsibilities at all times. A common misconception is that IAM is a one-time setup; in reality it requires continuous governance. Key takeaway: an IAM strategy maps identities to minimal permissions, centralizes reusable policies, and enforces reviews and MFA to maintain security over time.

Let's summarize the most important definitions to remember. First, an IAM user is a named identity with credentials — use it for people and external systems that require persistent access, secure it with MFA, and rotate any keys. Second, an IAM group is a collection of users used to manage permissions at scale; attach reusable policies to groups to simplify onboarding and offboarding. Third, an IAM role is an assumable identity that provides temporary credentials and is the recommended way to grant permissions to AWS services and federated users. Remember these core definitions as building blocks you will combine when designing secure access. As you recall these terms, ask yourself if current permissions in your account map to users, groups, and roles in a clear and auditable way. Finish with three more core reminders. First, an IAM policy is a JSON document specifying Effect, Action, Resource, and optional Condition; write policies that express only the actions and resources needed. Second, the principle of least privilege should guide every policy decision: narrow ARNs, prefer specific actions over wildcards, and test denied scenarios to confirm tight access. Third, enable Multi-Factor Authentication for root and privileged users to add a second verification factor that greatly reduces risk from stolen passwords or leaked keys. Combined, these ideas make access control auditable and resilient. Keep policies small, require second factors for critical operations, and use roles to avoid long-lived credentials.
